questions.stem: What is the answer given to the question 'Do we really need data modelling anymore?'
options: Modelling is obsolete in cloud-native platforms
Modelling is only needed for OLTP systems
There is no such thing as data without a model; every stored structure is a data model
Modelling is only needed when using schema-on-read
Modelling is optional once a data lake exists
questions.explanation: Every system that stores data follows a structure, explicit or implicit, and that structure is a data model; the question is what type of modelling suits the purpose.

questions.stem: Which type of system is Subjective Data Modelling commonly associated with?
options: Transactional OLTP systems using normalised structures such as 3NF
questions.explanation: Subjective Data Modelling is associated with transactional OLTP environments, typically relying on normalised structures such as Third Normal Form.

questions.stem: What question does Objective Data Modelling start from?
options: How does the system store data?
Which foreign keys enforce referential integrity?
How does the business need to analyse the data?
Which database vendor should be used?
questions.explanation: Objective modelling asks how the business needs to analyse data rather than how the system stores it, shifting the focus to analytical usability.

questions.stem: In the retail analytics example of Objective Data Modelling, which of these is stored in the central fact table?
options: Calendar attributes such as month and quarter
questions.explanation: The central fact table stores measures such as SalesAmount, Quantity and Discount, with dimensions for Time, Product, Geography and Customer.

questions.stem: Why is denormalisation deliberately introduced in Objective Data Modelling?
options: To simplify reporting and improve query performance
questions.explanation: In analytical environments denormalisation is introduced deliberately to simplify reporting and improve query performance.

questions.stem: Which phrase summarises what Subjective Data Modelling protects?
questions.explanation: Subjective Data Modelling protects operational truth, while Objective Data Modelling enables business understanding.

questions.stem: In which direction is Objective Data Modelling typically designed?
options: From the physical storage layer upwards
questions.explanation: Objective modelling is typically designed top-down, guided by the business questions that decision-makers need answered.

questions.stem: What happens to modelling in schema-on-read architectures if it is not done deliberately?
options: It is handled automatically by the storage format
It emerges accidentally through ad hoc transformations and inconsistent metric definitions
It is replaced by data governance
It becomes unnecessary because the data is flexible
questions.explanation: In modern architectures modelling does not disappear; it becomes implicit, and if not deliberate it emerges accidentally with conflicting metrics and duplicated KPIs.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed as a result of intentional modelling?
questions.explanation: Disagreeing reports are a symptom of accidental modelling; intentional modelling brings clear definitions, aligned KPIs, manageable governance and greater trust.

questions.stem: What is described as the real sign of architectural maturity?
options: Whether the organisation uses a star schema
Whether all data is in Third Normal Form
questions.explanation: The real sign of maturity is not whether data is modelled but whether it is modelled intentionally, integrating both subjective and objective perspectives.
